title: India Wants Access to Anthropic's Most Powerful AI. Washington Is Listening — Carefully.
excerpt: New Delhi is in talks to use Anthropic's Project Glasswing to stress-test India's critical digital infrastructure, as both countries navigate the geopolitics of frontier AI.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India seeks access to Anthropic's Project Glasswing for cybersecurity testing.
  • Discussions highlight deepening US-India AI partnership amid national security concerns.
  • India can conduct 60-70% of testing with existing AI models.
  • US lifted export controls on Anthropic's advanced AI models recently.
  • India's status as a tech partner is evolving, enhancing access to critical technologies.

India is negotiating with the United States to secure access to Anthropic's Project Glasswing, a consortium-backed initiative designed to probe and secure the world's most critical software systems. The request, confirmed by India's top technology official at a cybersecurity summit last week, marks one of the most concrete steps yet in the rapidly deepening US-India AI partnership — and one of the most sensitive. MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan, speaking at the Confederation of Indian Industry's Cybersecurity Summit, said India wants to use the advanced AI platform to "stress-test our systems on Anthropic's systems." Project Glasswing, launched by Anthropic in April, brings together Amazon Web Services, Apple, Broadcom, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Google, JPMorgan Chase, the Linux Foundation, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Palo Alto Networks in an unprecedented effort to identify vulnerabilities in the software that runs hospitals, power grids, and financial networks. But Krishnan was careful to note that India is not waiting. Around sixty to seventy per cent of the cybersecurity testing exercise can be carried out using AI models already available to India, he said. The Glasswing discussions are about filling the remaining gap — the frontier capabilities that only the most advanced models can deliver. ## The Bigger Picture: Pax Silica and Frontier Access The cybersecurity ask sits inside a much larger diplomatic conversation. At a closed-door roundtable organised by the Indian Embassy in Washington, Ambassador Vinay Mohan Kwatra, MeitY Secretary Krishnan, and US Deputy Under Secretary of Commerce Bill Guidera convened Indian and American companies working across semiconductors, critical minerals, and AI. ![Confederation of Indian Industry — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/89/CII_Headquarters_New_Delhi.jpg) > **""We continue to have ongoing conversations about this topic with our Indian friends," Helberg said."** The discussions, co-organised with the US-India Strategic Partnership Forum (USISPF) and Silverado Policy Accelerator, focused on addressing shared barriers for investment, creating durable demand signals, and expanding AI collaboration "at various levels, including frontier and application." US Under Secretary of Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg, speaking on the sidelines of the second Pax Silica Summit in Washington, confirmed that the two countries are engaged in "very sensitive national security discussions" about how to roll out Anthropic's most powerful models to trusted partners. "We continue to have ongoing conversations about this topic with our Indian friends," Helberg said. "Our intention is very much to continue a gradual, measured approach to how we release Anthropic's models in a way that is safe, both for ourselves but also for our Indian counterparts, as well as all our trusted partners, for our critical infrastructure, for our power grid." Helberg described India as one of the first major economies to join Pax Silica, the State Department's flagship initiative on AI and supply chain security, launched in December 2025. The programme seeks to build consensus among allies on secure supply chains spanning critical minerals, energy inputs, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, and AI infrastructure. ## Why This Matters Now ![Palo Alto Networks — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Palo_Alto_Networks_Headquarters_South_Side_2018.jpg/3840px-Palo_Alto_Networks_Headquarters_South_Side_2018.jpg)

The timing is not coincidental. The US Commerce Department just this week lifted export controls on Anthropic's most advanced Fable and Mythos models, less than three weeks after ordering their suspension over national security concerns. OpenAI has faced similar constraints: it delayed the full public launch of GPT-5.6 at the government's request, limiting access to vetted partners. Washington is simultaneously negotiating voluntary standards with major AI companies for new model releases, with an announcement possible as soon as next week. The standards would set benchmarks for advanced models, clarify timelines, and determine who can access them domestically and abroad. For India, which is rapidly building its own AI ecosystem — from semiconductor fabs to sovereign AI models — the question of frontier access is existential. Without access to the world's most powerful models for defensive testing, India's critical infrastructure could be vulnerable to attacks that exploit capabilities its own models cannot yet replicate. The broader diplomatic subtext is unmistakable: India is being treated as a first-tier technology partner, alongside the Five Eyes nations and a handful of other allies. This status, earned over years of Quad collaboration, iCET (Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology) progress, and growing semiconductor investments, is now translating into concrete access to technologies that most of the world cannot touch. ## The Diaspora Connection For the hundreds of thousands of Indian-origin engineers, researchers, and executives who work in American AI companies — including at Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI themselves — these negotiations carry a personal dimension. Many straddle both ecosystems, contributing to frontier AI development in the US while maintaining deep ties to India's technology sector. The US-India AI partnership is, in many ways, a diaspora story. Indian-American technologists have been instrumental in shaping America's AI leadership. Now, the frameworks being negotiated in Washington and New Delhi will determine whether that expertise can flow freely between the two countries — or whether geopolitical caution will create new walls in the one sector where India and America have the most to gain from openness.
